title: Suicide Risk: Ask Directly, Protect Immediately
bottomLine: When suicide risk is suspected, ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plan, intent, access to lethal means, recent attempts and protective factors. A patient with imminent risk should not be left alone while emergency psychiatric/safety evaluation is activated; remove hazards according to policy and use the least restrictive safe environment.
recognize: Current suicidal ideation with intent or plan
Recent attempt, rehearsal or escalating self-harm
Hopelessness, severe agitation, intoxication, psychosis or abrupt mood change can increase concern
Giving away possessions or saying goodbye can be warning behavior
assess: Ask directly and calmly about thoughts, plan, intent, means and timing
Assess recent attempt, substance use, command hallucinations, severe insomnia/agitation and supports
Use validated screening tools as aids—not replacements for clinical assessment
actions: Maintain observation level and environmental safety according to risk/policy
Activate psychiatric/emergency evaluation and communicate risk clearly at handoff
Remove or secure medications, sharps, ligature hazards and other means as directed
Document exact statements and actions objectively
diagnostics: No blood test rules suicide risk in or out; risk assessment is clinical and dynamic
medicationSafety: Early antidepressant treatment requires monitoring for worsening agitation or suicidal thinking, especially in younger patients
Sedating medications do not substitute for a safety plan and observation
redFlags: Attempt to leave despite imminent risk
teaching: Create a concrete safety plan before discharge and involve supportive people when appropriate and consent/legal rules permit
Limit access to lethal means as part of the plan
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN can ask direct suicide questions, maintain ordered observation and environmental safety, and escalate changes immediately. Final disposition/involuntary-hold decisions follow state law and authorized clinicians.
examTrap: Avoiding direct questions about suicide because asking is believed to 'put the idea in the patient's head.'
oneLinePearl: Ask directly; imminent risk means protect first and never leave the patient alone.
sourceBasis: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs/Department of Defense Suicide Risk Clinical Practice Guideline

title: Major Depression and SSRIs: Energy Can Improve Before Mood
bottomLine: Major depression can impair sleep, appetite, concentration, function and safety. Antidepressants usually take time for full benefit; monitor suicide risk closely, especially when energy or activation changes before hopelessness resolves. Teach adherence and do not stop SSRIs/SNRIs abruptly without a plan.
recognize: Persistent depressed mood or loss of interest plus neurovegetative/cognitive symptoms
Severe depression may include psychosis, catatonia or inability to maintain nutrition/self-care
Bipolar disorder should be considered when there is a history of mania/hypomania
assess: Suicide/self-neglect risk, sleep, appetite/weight, function and substance use
Medication adherence, activation/agitation and sexual/GI effects
Watch for manic symptoms after antidepressant initiation
actions: Maintain safety and therapeutic routine
Administer antidepressants on schedule and monitor response
Escalate emergent suicidality, mania, serotonin toxicity or severe functional decline
diagnostics: Diagnosis is clinical; thyroid, anemia, medication and substance causes may be evaluated when indicated
medicationSafety: SSRIs/SNRIs can cause GI/sexual effects, activation, hyponatremia and discontinuation symptoms
Serotonin syndrome risk rises with serotonergic combinations
Antidepressant monotherapy can worsen mania in susceptible bipolar patients
teaching: Benefit can take weeks, continue as prescribed, report severe agitation/suicidal change, and taper only with clinician guidance
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN monitors mood, safety and medication effects and reinforces the treatment plan. Diagnosis and regimen changes are prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Assuming the patient is safe because they suddenly have more energy even though hopelessness and suicidal thoughts remain.
oneLinePearl: In depression, improving energy can increase ability to act before mood catches up.
sourceBasis: American Psychiatric Association depression practice guidance

title: Acute Mania and Lithium: Reduce Stimulation, Protect Sleep and Hydration
bottomLine: Acute mania can cause sleep deprivation, impulsivity, aggression, dehydration, poor nutrition and unsafe judgment. Use a low-stimulation structured environment, concise limits, finger foods/fluids when needed and ordered mood-stabilizing therapy. With lithium, stable salt/fluid intake and renal monitoring are crucial; vomiting, coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion or worsening neurologic signs can indicate toxicity.
recognize: Decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, grandiosity, racing thoughts, distractibility, risky behavior
Severe mania may include psychosis or aggression
Lithium toxicity risk rises with dehydration, kidney dysfunction and interacting medications
assess: Safety, sleep, intake/hydration, impulsivity and psychosis
Lithium level when ordered plus renal/thyroid function and sodium
Medication interactions including NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs and thiazide diuretics
actions: Reduce stimulation and set brief consistent limits
Provide portable high-calorie food and fluids if the patient cannot sit for meals
Administer mood stabilizer/antipsychotic as ordered
Hold/clarify lithium and escalate suspected toxicity according to parameters
diagnostics: Lithium levels are interpreted with dose timing and clinical symptoms; toxicity can be clinically significant even before extreme levels
medicationSafety: Maintain consistent fluid and sodium intake unless another condition requires a prescribed restriction
Lithium is teratogenic-risk medication requiring pregnancy planning
Do not double missed lithium doses
teaching: Keep lab appointments, stable hydration/salt habits, and report vomiting/diarrhea or new interacting drugs
Do not stop mood stabilizers because mania feels productive or enjoyable
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN maintains safety/structure, monitors intake and medication effects, and reports toxicity or behavioral escalation. Lithium dosing and psychiatric regimen selection are prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Telling a lithium patient to drastically reduce dietary salt to be 'heart healthy' without considering lithium accumulation risk.
oneLinePearl: Lithium likes consistency: fluids, salt, kidneys and levels.
sourceBasis: American Psychiatric Association bipolar practice guidance

title: Schizophrenia: Safety, Reality-Based Communication, Antipsychotic Monitoring
bottomLine: With psychosis, acknowledge the patient's experience without validating the delusion, assess whether hallucinations command harm, reduce stimulation and maintain safety. Antipsychotics require monitoring for movement disorders, metabolic effects, orthostasis, QT risk and rare life-threatening syndromes.
recognize: Positive symptoms: hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thought/behavior
Negative symptoms: reduced affect, motivation, speech and social engagement
Command hallucinations require direct safety assessment
assess: Suicide/violence risk and command content
Ability to eat, drink, sleep and perform self-care
Movement symptoms, weight/BP/glucose/lipids and medication adherence
actions: Use brief calm reality-based statements
Do not argue extensively with delusions
Administer antipsychotics as ordered and support adherence
Escalate command hallucinations, severe agitation or medication emergencies
diagnostics: Diagnosis is clinical after medical/substance causes are considered
Metabolic and ECG monitoring depends on drug and patient risk
medicationSafety: Acute dystonia, akathisia and parkinsonism are extrapyramidal effects
Tardive dyskinesia requires ongoing movement screening
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome causes fever, severe rigidity, autonomic instability and altered mental status
teaching: Continue medication and follow metabolic/movement monitoring; report severe stiffness/fever, involuntary movements or fainting
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN provides therapeutic communication and safety monitoring and observes medication response. Regimen changes are psychiatric-prescriber directed.
examTrap: Telling the patient, 'Yes, the voices are real,' in an attempt to build trust.
oneLinePearl: Acknowledge the feeling, not the delusion; assess commands for danger.
sourceBasis: American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia

title: Clozapine: Infection Symptoms, Myocarditis, Seizures, Bowel Function
bottomLine: Clozapine can be highly effective for treatment-resistant schizophrenia but has serious risks including severe neutropenia, myocarditis/cardiomyopathy, seizures, severe constipation/ileus and metabolic effects. Fever or sore throat, chest symptoms, severe constipation/abdominal distention, seizure or marked sedation requires prompt assessment.
recognize: Infection symptoms can signal neutropenia
Myocarditis may present with chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia or flu-like symptoms
GI hypomotility can progress to obstruction/ileus
Seizure risk is dose/concentration related
assess: CBC/ANC monitoring per current prescribing requirements and clinical plan
Bowel frequency, abdominal symptoms, hydration and anticholinergic co-medications
Weight, glucose/lipids, BP and cardiac symptoms
actions: Administer exactly on schedule and report interrupted therapy because re-titration may be required
Escalate infection, myocarditis, seizure or severe GI symptoms
Use prescribed constipation-prevention plan
diagnostics: ANC and symptom-driven cardiac/GI evaluation are central; current FDA requirements should be checked because monitoring rules can change
medicationSafety: Abrupt restart at a previous high dose after an interruption can cause severe hypotension or other toxicity
Smoking changes can alter clozapine metabolism
Additive anticholinergic/sedating medications increase risk
teaching: Report infection and bowel symptoms early, keep lab follow-up, and tell the prescriber if smoking status changes or doses are missed for multiple days
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN monitors symptoms/labs and medication continuity and escalates serious adverse effects. Clozapine prescribing and re-titration are psychiatric-prescriber directed.
examTrap: Restarting the full prior clozapine dose after several missed days without prescriber/pharmacy clarification.
oneLinePearl: Clozapine: ANC, heart, seizures, bowels—and never casually restart after interruption.
sourceBasis: FDA Clozapine Prescribing and Safety Information

title: Panic Attack: Stay, Simplify, Breathe, Then Teach
bottomLine: During severe panic, stay with the patient, reduce stimulation, use short simple statements and coach slow breathing/grounding after medical emergencies are excluded. Complex teaching and insight work wait until anxiety decreases.
recognize: Sudden intense fear, palpitations, dyspnea, chest tightness, tremor, dizziness, derealization
First or atypical episodes can mimic cardiac, respiratory, endocrine or substance emergencies
Hyperventilation can intensify paresthesias and dizziness
assess: Immediate safety, vital signs and symptoms that require medical evaluation
Trigger, substance/caffeine/stimulant use and prior panic history
Suicide risk when anxiety is severe or comorbid depression exists
actions: Stay with patient and move to a quieter environment
Use calm brief directions and paced breathing/grounding
Administer PRN medication only when ordered and reassess sedation
After panic subsides, reinforce therapy/coping plan
diagnostics: Panic disorder is a clinical diagnosis after appropriate medical/substance causes are considered
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines can sedate and cause dependence and respiratory risk, especially with opioids/alcohol
SSRIs/SNRIs are common longer-term treatments but are not immediate rescue drugs
teaching: Practice coping skills when calm, limit excess stimulants, and follow psychotherapy/medication plan
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN provides therapeutic support, basic medical screening and ordered medication and escalates atypical/emergency findings.
examTrap: Trying to teach a detailed cognitive-behavioral worksheet while the patient is at peak panic and cannot process information.
oneLinePearl: Peak panic needs presence and simple grounding; teaching comes later.
sourceBasis: American Psychiatric Association anxiety/panic treatment principles

title: PTSD: Trauma-Informed Care Avoids Recreating Loss of Control
bottomLine: PTSD can include intrusion, avoidance, negative mood/cognition and hyperarousal after trauma. Use trauma-informed care: explain before touching, offer choices when possible, avoid forced disclosure, screen safety/substance use and support evidence-based psychotherapy and medication plans.
recognize: Nightmares/flashbacks and distress at reminders
Avoidance
Hypervigilance/startle/irritability and sleep disturbance
Depression, substance use and suicide risk commonly coexist
assess: Safety/suicide risk, sleep, substance use and functional impairment
Triggers and preferences for care
Current psychotherapy and medication adherence
actions: Provide predictable respectful interactions and permission/choice where possible
Ground during flashbacks without arguing about the experience
Support trauma-focused psychotherapy and prescribed medications
Escalate imminent safety concerns
diagnostics: Diagnosis is clinical; screening tools identify probable PTSD but do not replace assessment
medicationSafety: SSRIs/SNRIs are common medication options
Routine benzodiazepine treatment for PTSD is generally discouraged because of harms and limited benefit
teaching: Recovery does not require forced retelling; evidence-based trauma-focused therapy is available and symptoms are treatable
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN uses trauma-informed communication and safety monitoring and reinforces treatment. Trauma processing therapy is provided by appropriately trained clinicians.
examTrap: Pressuring the patient to describe the trauma in detail during routine nursing care because talking is assumed to be automatically therapeutic.
oneLinePearl: Trauma-informed care restores choice and safety rather than forcing disclosure.
sourceBasis: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for PTSD

title: Eating Disorders and Refeeding: The Heart Can Be at Risk
bottomLine: Severe restrictive eating or purging can cause bradycardia, hypotension, electrolyte disturbance, arrhythmia and organ dysfunction. Refeeding a severely malnourished patient can cause dangerous phosphate, potassium, magnesium and fluid shifts, so nutrition restoration requires a monitored structured plan.
recognize: Restriction, binge/purge behavior, intense weight/shape preoccupation may be present
Medical instability can occur at any body size
Refeeding syndrome risk rises with significant malnutrition and prolonged low intake
assess: Vitals including orthostasis when appropriate, ECG, hydration and temperature
Potassium, magnesium, phosphate, glucose and renal/liver tests as ordered
Suicide/self-harm risk and purging/laxative/diuretic behaviors
actions: Follow supervised nutrition/refeeding plan
Replace electrolytes/thiamine as ordered and monitor closely
Use structured post-meal support without punitive confrontation
Escalate severe bradycardia, arrhythmia, syncope or electrolyte instability
diagnostics: BMI alone does not determine medical severity
ECG and electrolyte abnormalities help determine instability
medicationSafety: QT-prolonging drugs can be higher risk with electrolyte abnormalities
Laxative/diuretic misuse worsens volume/electrolytes
teaching: Recovery requires medical, nutritional and psychological treatment; avoid weight-shaming or praise tied to disordered behaviors
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN follows the structured meal/safety/monitoring plan and reports instability. Calorie advancement and electrolyte protocols are medical/dietitian-team directed.
examTrap: Starting unrestricted high-calorie feeding without electrolyte monitoring in a severely malnourished patient.
oneLinePearl: Refeeding saves nutrition but can destabilize electrolytes—restore carefully.
sourceBasis: APA Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders

title: Alcohol Withdrawal: Seizures and Delirium Can Escalate Fast
bottomLine: Alcohol withdrawal can progress from tremor, anxiety, sweating and tachycardia to seizures and withdrawal delirium. Identify last drink and prior severe withdrawal, use a validated symptom protocol when appropriate, give benzodiazepines as ordered, provide thiamine and correct fluids/electrolytes, and escalate delirium, seizure or autonomic instability.
recognize: Tremor, anxiety, insomnia, nausea, tachycardia and hypertension
Withdrawal seizures can occur early
Withdrawal delirium includes severe agitation/confusion, autonomic instability and hallucinations
assess: Last alcohol use, daily amount, prior seizures/delirium, other sedatives
Vitals, mental status, seizure risk and hydration
Glucose, magnesium, potassium, liver and other labs as ordered
actions: Seizure/fall precautions
Administer benzodiazepine based on protocol/order and reassess
Give thiamine and nutrition/electrolyte support as ordered
Escalate severe withdrawal for monitored/critical care
diagnostics: Withdrawal is a clinical diagnosis; blood alcohol can still be positive while withdrawal begins in dependent patients
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines can depress respiration, especially with opioids/other sedatives
Thiamine should be provided promptly; life-threatening hypoglycemia is treated immediately and should not be delayed solely to give thiamine first
teaching: Medically supervised withdrawal is safer for high-risk dependence; connect patients with evidence-based treatment for alcohol use disorder
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN can score symptoms and administer protocol medication where authorized, with frequent reassessment. Severe withdrawal requires higher-acuity escalation.
examTrap: Assuming a positive blood alcohol level means the patient cannot already be withdrawing.
oneLinePearl: Alcohol withdrawal is a CNS hyperactivity emergency—watch seizures and delirium.
sourceBasis: ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management

title: Opioid Overdose: Ventilate, Naloxone, Watch for Recurrence
bottomLine: Opioid overdose kills through respiratory depression. If the patient is not breathing normally, activate emergency response, support ventilation/airway, give naloxone as indicated and repeat per protocol, then continue observation because naloxone may wear off before the opioid.
recognize: Slow/shallow/absent breathing, decreased consciousness and often pinpoint pupils
Cyanosis or snoring/gurgling can indicate airway compromise
Long-acting or potent synthetic opioids may require repeated naloxone
assess: Responsiveness, breathing, pulse, oxygenation and airway
Medication/substance history and co-ingestants
Reassess frequently after naloxone for recurrent sedation
actions: Call emergency response and provide rescue breathing/BVM/CPR according to pulse and breathing
Administer naloxone via available route
Place breathing patient in recovery position when appropriate and monitor
Treat recurrent respiratory depression and arrange emergency evaluation
diagnostics: Do not wait for toxicology confirmation before treating a compatible respiratory emergency
medicationSafety: Naloxone can precipitate acute withdrawal but restoration of breathing is the priority
Sedating co-ingestants may limit response to naloxone
teaching: Patients and families at opioid risk should have naloxone and know rescue breathing/EMS activation; medication for opioid use disorder reduces overdose risk
scopeAndDelegation: Naloxone can be administered under emergency/standing orders in many settings; follow local law/policy. Airway support and EMS activation should not be delayed.
examTrap: Waiting to see whether the patient wakes up before providing ventilation to a patient with dangerously slow breathing.
oneLinePearl: Opioid overdose: breathing first, naloxone fast, monitor after.
sourceBasis: SAMHSA Opioid Overdose Prevention and Response Toolkit

title: Stimulant Intoxication: Hyperthermia, Agitation, Chest Pain, Seizure
bottomLine: Cocaine or methamphetamine toxicity can produce severe agitation, hypertension, tachycardia, hyperthermia, chest pain, dysrhythmia, stroke and seizure. Reduce stimulation, protect staff/patient, monitor temperature/cardiovascular/neuro status and give protocol-directed sedation/cooling while escalating organ-threatening symptoms.
recognize: Agitation, paranoia, diaphoresis, mydriasis, tachycardia/hypertension
Chest pain or focal neurologic symptoms may reflect acute ischemia/stroke
Hyperthermia and severe agitation can cause rhabdomyolysis and acidosis
assess: Airway/breathing, BP/HR/rhythm, temperature and neuro status
Chest pain, seizure, trauma and co-ingestants
CK, renal/electrolytes, ECG/troponin and other tests as ordered
actions: Use de-escalation and low-stimulation environment when possible
Administer benzodiazepine sedation and active cooling according to emergency plan
Treat chest pain, seizure, hyperthermia and hypertensive emergency through the appropriate pathway
diagnostics: Urine toxicology can support exposure but should not delay treatment
Clinical syndrome and organ injury determine urgency
medicationSafety: Sedatives require respiratory monitoring
Medication selection for stimulant-associated cardiovascular emergencies should follow current emergency/toxicology guidance rather than outdated one-size-fits-all rules
teaching: Offer evidence-based substance-use treatment and harm-reduction counseling after stabilization
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN provides monitored supportive care and protocol medications and escalates organ-threatening toxicity. Restraint use follows least-restrictive safety rules.
examTrap: Treating severe stimulant agitation as purely behavioral and missing hyperthermia, chest pain or neurologic injury.
oneLinePearl: Stimulants can cook, seize, stroke and ischemize—check the body, not just behavior.
sourceBasis: ASAM/AAAP Clinical Practice Guideline on Management of Stimulant Use Disorder

title: Therapeutic Communication: Open, Specific, Nonjudgmental
bottomLine: Therapeutic communication helps the patient describe experience and make safe decisions without being judged, interrogated or falsely reassured. Use open-ended prompts, reflection, clarification, silence and specific observations; avoid 'why' interrogation, unsolicited advice, changing the subject or promises you cannot keep.
recognize: A patient's behavior often communicates distress even when words do not
Silence can be therapeutic when the nurse remains present
Direct safety questions are appropriate when risk is suspected
assess: What the patient is saying and not saying
Affect, behavior, culture/language, cognitive capacity and sensory needs
Whether privacy or a qualified interpreter is needed
actions: Use one question at a time and allow processing time
Name observations without assumptions
Clarify ambiguous statements and ask directly about safety when relevant
Set respectful limits on unsafe behavior
redFlags: Inability to understand due to delirium/intoxication
teaching: Use teach-back rather than asking only 'Do you understand?'
scopeAndDelegation: Therapeutic communication is within every nurse's role, but counseling/psychotherapy that requires specialized licensure is not automatically a PN/LVN function.
examTrap: Saying 'Everything will be fine' to a frightened patient when the outcome is uncertain.
oneLinePearl: Ask, listen, clarify, reflect—do not judge or promise.
